consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on the same primary meaning: belief (pisteuo) is saving faith—personal trust in, reliance upon, and commitment to God/Christ as the means of receiving salvation and eternal life, explicitly distinguished from mere intellectual assent. Alternatives noted include assent-only belief (as an inadequate foil), belief as allegiance/faithfulness/'obedience of faith' (flagged as a minority scholarly view), belief as divine gift vs. human response, and faith inseparable from works in Catholic/Orthodox/Wesleyan readings.
book_summary: The book defines belief as 'to obey because it is the truth'—an obedient response rather than bare assent—anchoring this in the lexical observation that the New Testament opposite of 'believe' is apeitheo, 'to disobey' (John 3:36), and in Romans 10:16's parallel between obeying the gospel and believing the report. The book explicitly sets this against the commonly taught view of belief as personal trust functioning as the instrument that receives salvation.
rationale: The book's central claim recasts belief from trust-that-receives to obedience-that-responds. This is not merely a sharpening of the consensus: mainstream (especially Protestant) teaching deliberately distinguishes faith from obedience/works as the receiving instrument of salvation, and the book's own common-view note signals it is displacing that teaching. The obedience/allegiance reading does appear in the blind responses, but only as an expressly minority alternative (Responses A, B, C all mark 'obedience of faith'/allegiance as minority prominence). Elevating a minority alternative to the primary definition, while demoting the dominant 'personal trust as instrument' view, fits DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the allegiance/obedience reading is recognizably represented in the consensus landscape.
strongest_objection: The book's reading could be classed as REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: it does not deny trust but specifies its character, and the consensus responses themselves acknowledge the believe/disobey contrast in John 3:36 and the 'obedience of faith' as an existing (if minority) Christian interpretation—so the book may be sharpening the settled view rather than displacing it. Additionally, the two printed citations genuinely exhibit the believe/obey interchange (apeitheo in John 3:36; obey/believe parallelism in Rom 10:16), so the lexical core of the claim has real textual footing even if two verses cannot establish that belief means obedience across Scripture.
